name: AI2 Reasoning Challenge (ARC)
description: A dataset consisting of 7,787 natural, grade-school science multiple-choice questions authored for human standardized tests, partitioned into a Challenge Set and an Easy Set, along with the ARC Corpus of 14M science-related sentences and baseline models to encourage research in advanced question answering.
creator: Peter Clark, Isaac Cowhey, Oren Etzioni, Tushar Khot, Ashish Sabharwal, Carissa Schoenick, Oyvind Tafjord
citeAs: Peter Clark, Isaac Cowhey, Oren Etzioni, Tushar Khot, Ashish Sabharwal, Carissa Schoenick, Oyvind Tafjord. Think you have Solved Question Answering? Try ARC, the AI2 Reasoning Challenge. arXiv:1803.05457v1, 2018.
rai:dataCollection: The ARC dataset was assembled through several months of extensive search and investigation to obtain publicly releasable natural science questions authored for standardized tests. The dataset consists of 7,787 non-diagram, multiple-choice science questions drawn from a variety of sources and partitioned into a Challenge Set and an Easy Set. The Challenge Set was operationally defined as questions answered incorrectly by both a retrieval-based solver and a PMI-based co-occurrence solver. In addition, the ARC Corpus was created by using a major search engine to run a large series of automatically constructed science-related queries based on about 100 hand-written templates for 80 science topics; top documents were collected, deduplicated, stripped to text, and chunked into sentences, then augmented with the AristoMini corpus.
rai:dataCollectionType: Document analysis, Software Collection, Web Scraping, Others
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data sources for the question set were standardized test science questions from a variety of sources, including state assessment programs and an anonymous content partner ('Mercury'). The ARC Corpus raw data came from Web documents retrieved via a major search engine using science-topic query templates, plus the AristoMini corpus containing Wiktionary definitions, Simple Wikipedia science articles, and additional science sentences collected from the Web.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Questions were sorted into a Challenge Set of 2,590 questions and an Easy Set of 5,197 questions based on whether both the IR solver and PMI solver failed to answer them correctly. For the ARC Corpus, collected documents were deduplicated, stripped down to text, and chunked into sentences; the corpus was then augmented with AristoMini.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For the ARC Corpus, the top several documents from each search were collected and deduplicated, document content was stripped down to capture just the text, and the resulting text was chunked into sentences. In entailment-based baseline processing, retrieved sentences were filtered to remove long sentences (>300 characters), sentences with negation, and noisy sentences.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The dataset contains multiple-choice science questions authored for human standardized tests, with correct answer options provided as part of those test questions. No new human annotation process for ARC question labels is described. The paper also reports a sampled analysis of 100 Challenge questions to enumerate broad classes of knowledge and reasoning types, and an informal analysis of random samples of collected documents and questions for corpus relevance and coverage.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The paper notes that categorization of knowledge and reasoning types was based on a sample of 100 questions and that the relative sizes of categories are necessarily approximate because assigning the main challenge exhibited by different questions requires subjective judgment. It also reports informal sampled analyses: approximately 75% of a random sample of 805 collected documents were judged science relevant, and the ARC Corpus appeared to mention knowledge relevant to approximately 95% of Challenge questions from a random sample analysis.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The ARC Dataset, Corpus, three baseline neural models, and leaderboard are available at http://data.allenai.org/arc. The paper states that for up-to-date results, users should see the ARC leaderboard.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Question grade level is included, ranging from 3rd grade to 9th, corresponding to students typically of age 8 through 13 years.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to encourage AI research on question answering that requires reasoning, commonsense knowledge, and deeper text comprehension rather than surface-level retrieval. The authors present ARC as a challenge to the community and argue that progress on ARC would be a significant step forward for AI research.
rai:dataBiases: The paper discusses bias in prior standardized-test datasets where scores become dominated by simple algorithms such as information retrieval and statistical correlations, which biases research toward incrementally improving those algorithms rather than addressing harder AI challenges. It also notes retrieval bias in baseline systems: underlying IR methods favor sentences very similar to the question and disfavor sets of sentences that only partially match individually but together explain the correct answer.
rai:dataLimitations: The operational definition of a Challenge question only approximates the informal goal of being a hard question. The corpus relevance analysis is informal and sampled. The authors note that exploiting the ARC Corpus is not trivial even when relevant knowledge is present indirectly. They also note that baseline methods are limited by retrieval strategies that favor lexical overlap and may miss multi-fact reasoning. For entailment conversion, the simple question-to-assertion method can produce ungrammatical sentences, and a more sophisticated rule-based approach was left to future work.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for advanced question answering research and benchmarking. It is partitioned into train/dev/test splits for both Challenge and Easy sets. The Challenge Set is designed to evaluate methods requiring more advanced reasoning, while the Easy Set contains the remaining questions. The ARC Corpus is released as an optional supporting corpus; systems are not restricted to using it.
